Its stock dropped almost 10% in one day, and recent news about CEO Jensen Huang being a possible target of spying sent the stock down even further.The timing here works out to be just one week before Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Is it a buy ahead of that report? A swath of stocks took a hit after the election as numerous Democratic candidates who have promised to push for a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) development and the AI data center build-out won their races. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Some AI stocks rose on the news, including Amazon, since the market has been worried about the extraordinary amount of money it is laying out on data centers, and investors welcomed the possibility of it slowing its spending spree. Nvidia, though, benefits from AI spend, which is why its share price dropped so quickly. It's the main provider of the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power AI workloads, with up to 95% of the data center GPU market. Wall Street expects the company's revenue to increase 91% this year, and Nvidia management has already provided guidance for a 70% sales increase next year. It called that a "supply-constrained outlook." However, if AI companies are compelled to slow down their build-outs and model development, reduced spending could hurt their chances of making that happen. For the fiscal third quarter, which ended Oct. 25, management is guiding for about 90% sales growth, and Wall Street expects $2.47 in earnings per share, up from $1.30 last year. Nvidia tends to easily beat expectations, and the stock generally rises after its earnings reports, but not always. One area the market will be watching is gross margin. Nvidia is guiding for about 74%, but that's lower than recent levels. NVDA Gross Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts That decline is connected to the rising cost of memory chips, which have been plaguing many AI companies. At the current price, Nvidia stock trades at a low valuation of 11 times next year's expected earnings. If management provides updates that expectations for next year haven't changed for the worse, the stock is likely to rise; a lower P/E ratio usually indicates that the market doesn't think a company can keep growing earnings at a fast rate. If it can, the P/E ratio should rise. In other words, the market's reaction is likely to take more notice of guidance than results, which are usually stellar. Long term, Nvidia has an excellent business, and its products remain critical components of AI development, which isn't going away. Now could be a good time for long-term investors to scoop up shares, but expect periods of volatility as AI stocks go through change. And even if you can stomach those ups and downs, at this point, I wouldn't give Nvidia a prime position in your portfolio. We just published a list of the 10 Stocks Analysts Just Downgraded and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) ranked 10th on this list. Wall Street has had a rough start to November. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% on November 5, its steepest one-day drop in 19 months, and slid into a correction, more than 10% below its October 6 record close. The semiconductor index lost more than 12% that day, and about $3 trillion in value was erased from S&P 500 companies. Fear of tighter rules on AI drove much of the rout. Democratic wins in the November elections raised concerns that stricter regulation could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure, and the stocks tied to data centers took the hardest hit. Investors who had been paying up for AI growth suddenly had to ask how much of that growth could be stopped by politics. Not everyone saw the drop as a verdict on the AI trade. Jed Ellerbroek of Argent Capital Management described the selling as a capitulation phase for data center beneficiaries, meaning forced selling that often marks a low. A Wall Street research shop, Yardeni, argued that political pushback on data centers amounts to "speed bumps, not roadblocks, even though Wall Street seems to be pricing in the latter." The economy did not offer a cushion. Payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, far above the 65,000 to 70,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate stood at 4.1%. That kept a December rate hike in play, and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin have both hinted that higher rates could be on the table. Our ranking of oversold AI stocks where Wall Street analysts see 50%+ upside looks at the corner of the market that sold off the most. On Monday, strategists led by Beata Manthey cut US stocks and the global technology sector to neutral and raised European stocks outside the UK to overweight. Manthey warned that positioning in stocks "could reset lower into net-short territory." The S&P 500 had its biggest weekly loss since April 2025, which helps explain why many investors are looking for cheaper places to put money. You might also be interested in our list of affordable stocks Wall Street analysts like. Stocks bounced back on Monday. By midday, the Dow was up about 2%, the S&P 500 about 2.3%, and the Nasdaq about 2.6%. Inflation data due later this week is the next big test for the market and for the Federal Reserve's rate path, and analysts have kept reshuffling their ratings as the numbers move. Nvidia made it to our list because it has an average upside potential of 88%. However, Stefan Chang, an analyst at Aletheia Capital, cut Nvidia to Hold from Buy on November 9 and withdrew his $340 price target. His worry is not demand for the chips but the money Nvidia has promised to the companies buying them. Chang said an AI Computing Partner program has pushed the company's financial commitments up more than tenfold, to $165 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and he called the funding picture for smaller AI cloud builders opaque. He also pointed to a guarantee the company gave on an Ohio data center. Nvidia designs the chips that run most large AI data centers, and the business behind the worry is still growing fast. Revenue came in at $96.2 billion last quarter, up 106% from a year earlier, and Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the AI infrastructure buildout is "at full steam." The company guided to $108.0 billion for the current quarter without counting any Data Center compute revenue from China. Fresh numbers arrive when Nvidia reports again next week. To be clear, these are still just allegations and nothing has been proven -- Reuters said that it could not independently verify the report -- but The Information is a highly reputable news outlet and its reporting should be taken seriously. It took five minutes for Tuesday's hot inflation report to knock stocks lower, and Nvidia (NVDA) never recovered. The chipmaker hasn't been sold this hard, this fast since 2019, but the typical S&P 500 stock finished the day flat. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) closed down about 0.4% Tuesday after an afternoon rebound, shedding about $250 billion in market value according to Yahoo Finance calculations. The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) also fell about 0.4%, while the equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP), which gives every company the same weight, finished flat. Nvidia closed down about 6%, as the scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang drags on. Its relative strength index, a gauge of how fast and how far a stock has moved, sank to 24 out of a possible 100 — its most oversold reading since June 2019. Read more: Nvidia stock drops as spy fiasco involving CEO Jensen Huang raises broader risk concerns Memory makers Micron (MU) and SanDisk (SNDK) and chip designer Arm (ARM) fell roughly 1% to 3%. AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) rose, adding to Monday's surge. The longer view is starker. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks has lost nearly $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, roughly a quarter of its worth. That's more than the roughly $2.7 trillion the entire S&P 500 has shed over the same stretch, even though the basket includes some companies outside the index. Tuesday's trigger was a hotter-than-expected October consumer price index. S&P 500 futures fell about 0.5% in the five minutes after the 8:30 a.m. ET release, on volume many times the morning's norm. Nasdaq 100 futures briefly erased their losses by 10 a.m., slid again, then recovered much of the damage in the afternoon. Bonds felt it too. The 5-year Treasury yield (^FVX) posted its biggest one-day jump since September, and the 10-year (^TNX) briefly topped 5% as traders raised bets on a December rate hike. BofA's Savita Subramanian sees the bigger risk in the S&P 500 itself. "We're not particularly bullish on the index. I think the index itself is a bit risky," the head of US equity and quantitative strategy at BofA Securities told Yahoo Finance on Tuesday. "What's the most crowded equity ticker in the world? It's the S&P index." The typical stock looks nothing like the index. The equal-weighted S&P 500 is up about 4% since Oct. 6 and closed at a record on Nov. 4. Some see Nvidia's slide as a chance to buy. "I think if [CEO Jensen Huang] stays, then this is going to prove to be overdone. And you know this will be a strong buying opportunity," Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon said Monday on Yahoo Finance's "Deirdre Bosa Live." Veteran trader Michael Martin isn't convinced. title: NVDA is ‘silly cheap,’ now is ‘the opportunity of an absolute lifetime’ – analysts - TradingView
content: Nvidia shares NVDA may be “silly cheap” right now, presenting a compelling buying opportunity despite near-term uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, according to Mizuho Securities tech analyst Jordan Klein. In an interview with CNBC, Klein pointed to the chipmaker's forward price-to-earnings multiple dropping below 10x as evidence of extreme undervaluation. Such depressed multiples are "usually reserved for companies that have structural impairments, or a business that is in secular decline, and we know that's not the case here," Klein explained. The stock has been derating for some time, with earnings growing significantly faster than the share price, and is now discounting considerable uncertainty related to both post-election concerns and questions surrounding Huang's leadership. Klein acknowledged that the potential loss of Huang represents a significant risk for the company. "He's not only a visionary and a leader for the company, but for the entire technology industry and the AI industry as a whole," Klein said, adding that in his view, Huang is "irreplaceable in the minds of investors." The analyst noted that while Nvidia NVDA has a deep bench of talent, the unknown timeline of the ongoing situation remains the biggest concern for market participants. Julian Emanuel, senior managing director at Evercore ISI, offered a more optimistic perspective. His firm recently placed Nvidia NVDA on its list of AI stocks to buy for next year, and Emanuel suggested the current weakness could be "the opportunity of an absolute lifetime" if leadership remains sound. Emanuel also pointed to broader market dynamics as encouraging for tech investors. Technology stocks as a whole VGT, XLK, IYW are now trading cheaper than the S&P 500 (SP500) for the first time in more than a decade, he noted. title: Jensen Huang’s departure would shave 30% off Nvidia’s stock price, tech bull Dan Ives says - Business Insider
content: Jensen Huang is worth about 30% of Nvidia's total value. That's according to prominent tech bull Dan Ives, who said on Tuesday that Huang's departure from the AI chip titan would whittle its value by nearly a third. Huang is embroiled in a scandal related to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, has been an executive at Singaporean data firm Megaspeed, a company with ties to big Chinese tech firms. If Huang were to depart, Ives said that Nvidia stock would fall 25% to 30%, implying a drop to around $122 per share. "We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25%-30%) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs both in the US and globally especially for China," Ives, a senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note. Nvidia shares were hit by a broader panic in the AI trade last week, with Huang's affair the latest headwind pushing against the price. The stock has tumbled 25% from its early October peak, and is down 8% year-to-date. Ives pointed to the "key man risk," the idea that much of Nvidia's value is pegged to the visibility and image of Jensen Huang. There is no publicly known succession plan at Nvidia. "Jensen is the core DNA of Nvidia and its AI success and ambitions are heavily tied to him staying on as CEO. Jensen is not replaceable," Ives said. "There is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO." The dilemma extends to the broader stock market and the economy, as well. Who would have guessed that a private scandal involving NVIDIA NVDA CEO Jensen Huang would escalate into a potential national security crisis, triggering a multi-billion-dollar stock market rout? Indeed, the company's shares tumbled more than 8% at Monday's open before closing down 4.3% on Nov. 9, erasing roughly $193 billion from NVIDIA's market value. The significant sell-off followed Jensen Huang's public admission of an extramarital affair and the board's swift launch of an independent investigation. Independent directors are now probing whether the tech pioneer was the unwitting target of a foreign espionage campaign tied to Alice Huang, a Chinese data center executive whose firm is accused of illicitly smuggling restricted U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) chips to Beijing. For investors weighing exposure to Nvidia, the latest turn of events demands a moment to reposition their portfolio around this turmoil. Rather than owning the stock outright, channeling exposure through Nvidia-heavy exchange-traded funds (ETFs) may let investors capture the stock's AI growth story while adding a layer of cushioning against this kind of headline risk. But before identifying those funds, one must understand a single line of logic: will this event in the CEO's personal life affect the stock only in the short term, or will it affect the company's long-term governance — and how can ETF investment act as a shield against heavy losses amid the current turn of events? Nvidia's position as the leader in AI-accelerated computing remains intact. As far as the company's fundamentals are concerned, in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues surged 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, while operating income soared 124%. The company's central role in AI infrastructure, reinforced by expanding alliances — such as with SK Telecom and Rebellions, integrating third-party chips via NVLink Fusion — deepens its economic moat. These factors surely make NVDA one of the most sought-after stocks in the tech industry. Yet, the recently launched investigation might be damaging for this tech giant, not necessarily due to the CEO's alleged personal conduct, but because it highlights Nvidia's succession uncertainty and substantial key-person risk. Huang, 63, is not only the face of the company but also its top-down operational core. Internal records reviewed by CNBC reveal that Huang had between 33 and 60 direct reports as of early November, with no publicly identified successor or clear second-in-command being groomed to assume leadership. In this context, Melius Research noted that investors had expected Huang to lead Nvidia for at least another decade. However, the lack of a clear succession plan could prompt investors to assign a higher risk premium to the stock if concerns emerge about his ability to continue leading the company. That said, NVIDIA's underlying fundamentals remain strong, supported by sustained demand for its AI chips, a competitive advantage stemming from its CUDA software ecosystem and a robust balance sheet that provides financial flexibility to support future growth. While the reported investigation could weigh on Nvidia's shares in the near term, it does not necessarily undermine the company's long-term earnings potential or its appeal as a growth-oriented investment. Despite the solid growth opportunities that NVIDIA has to offer, no one can deny the fact that the stock's leadership uncertainty has become a near-term threat in the recent turn of events. Investing directly in Nvidia at this juncture could expose investors to heightened uncertainty surrounding Huang's leadership and the outcome of the reported investigation. These ETFs typically hold Nvidia alongside Microsoft, Apple, Broadcom, and other tech or AI beneficiaries. The timing is particularly interesting. Technology stocks have experienced considerable volatility amid concerns about AI infrastructure spending, potential regulation, and whether the industry's growth is sustainable. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. I think investors should be focusing on what Nvidia's upcoming earnings reveal about the underlying business. Based on management's latest guidance, there's reason to believe the growth story remains intact. During the company's fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, representing a 106% increase year over year. Data center revenue reached $89 billion, increasing 117% annually. Meanwhile, earnings per share (EPS) climbed 128% to $2.46, while the company's gross margin reached 75%. What's even more encouraging is the company expects more growth. Management guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%, representing roughly 89% growth compared with the same quarter last year. Wall Street's expectations are slightly higher. Analysts are projecting approximately $108.9 billion in revenue and EPS of $2.47. That would represent roughly 91% revenue growth and 90% earnings growth year over year. Importantly, Nvidia's guidance does not assume any data center revenue from China. Nvidia's growth isn't just the result of companies experimenting with AI. The company is heavily embedded with capital expenditure (capex) commitments from cloud computing providers, frontier model developers, and enterprises building production-scale applications. Companies including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI are expanding their data center footprints to support AI training and inference. These investments translate directly into demand for Nvidia's GPUs, networking equipment, and integrated computing systems. The company's Blackwell architecture is an important component of hyperscaler infrastructure, supporting AI training and inference workloads. Meanwhile, Nvidia's new Vera Rubin platform is in full production, with deployments underway across cloud providers including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and CoreWeave. Rubin combines GPU computing with Nvidia's Vera CPUs and high-speed networking systems. Training generative models requires enormous levels of compute. However, inference -- the process of generating responses and performing tasks using trained models -- is now also becoming a major source of computing demand. As AI applications become more sophisticated, the amount of compute required to serve end users will increase substantially. Nvidia is positioning its GPUs, CPUs, networking systems, and CUDA software to capture more spending across various layers of AI workloads. Beyond Nvidia's financial results, investors are navigating a new source of uncertainty. Nvidia's board of directors recently launched an independent investigation following reports that Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair, while the intelligence allegations remain under investigation and Nvidia says it has no reason to believe trade secrets were compromised. The development has weighed on investor sentiment, particularly because Huang has played such a central role in Nvidia's growth. However, investors should not confuse questions surrounding corporate leadership with evidence that demand for Nvidia's products is going away. Those are separate issues. I'll be watching three things particularly closely: data center revenue growth, gross margin, and management's fourth-quarter outlook. If Nvidia delivers another strong quarter but offers disappointing guidance, investors could interpret that as evidence that AI infrastructure spending is beginning to moderate. Conversely, results that exceed expectations alongside accelerating demand for Vera Rubin could help restore confidence in the company's growth trajectory. Data center revenue reached $89 billion, increasing 117% annually. Meanwhile, earnings per share (EPS) climbed 128% to $2.46, while the company's gross margin reached 75%. Management guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%, representing roughly 89% growth compared with the same quarter last year. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Nvidia's growth isn't just the result of companies experimenting with AI. The company is heavily embedded with capital expenditure (capex) commitments from cloud computing providers, frontier model developers, and enterprises building production-scale applications. Companies including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI are expanding their data center footprints to support AI training and inference. These investments translate directly into demand for Nvidia's GPUs, networking equipment, and integrated computing systems. The company's Blackwell architecture is an important component of hyperscaler infrastructure, supporting AI training and inference workloads. Meanwhile, Nvidia's new Vera Rubin platform is in full production, with deployments underway across cloud providers including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and CoreWeave. Rubin combines GPU computing with Nvidia's Vera CPUs and high-speed networking systems. Training generative models requires enormous levels of compute. However, inference -- the process of generating responses and performing tasks using trained models -- is now also becoming a major source of computing demand. As AI applications become more sophisticated, the amount of compute required to serve end users will increase substantially. Nvidia is positioning its GPUs, CPUs, networking systems, and CUDA software to capture more spending across various layers of AI workloads. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair, while the intelligence allegations remain under investigation and Nvidia says it has no reason to believe trade secrets were compromised. The development has weighed on investor sentiment, particularly because Huang has played such a central role in Nvidia's growth. However, investors should not confuse questions surrounding corporate leadership with evidence that demand for Nvidia's products is going away. Those are separate issues. I'll be watching three things particularly closely: data center revenue growth, gross margin, and management's fourth-quarter outlook. If Nvidia delivers another strong quarter but offers disappointing guidance, investors could interpret that as evidence that AI infrastructure spending is beginning to moderate. Conversely, results that exceed expectations alongside accelerating demand for Vera Rubin could help restore confidence in the company's growth trajectory. "It's bizarre," one former sell-side analyst told me. Having been a member of the consensus analyst community, I can tell you there could be several reasons for the initial silence. One, a sharp critique of Huang could get an analyst cut off from access to management. Considering how widely owned Nvidia's stock is and how important the company is to investment banks (acquisitions, stock buybacks, financings, etc.), being cut off isn't exactly great for job security. Two, many of the analysts who cover Nvidia have known Huang for decades and have a relationship with him. They could be waiting to see how this shakes out. Three, there could be little appetite to publish anything before the board's investigation concludes. And lastly, some may remain fixated on Nvidia's pure fundamentals, which still look strong into 2027 even if Huang isn't CEO. Being the key player in the AI chip boom offers that luxury. To be clear, analysts should be very concerned, as it's Huang who has powered the Nvidia discounted free cash flow model that has minted money for the clients of the biggest sell-side shops. Huang has made Wall Street stock analysts look like stock-picking heroes in the process! But there is a real chance he won't be leading the company and driving its financial results for much longer, given the delicate predicament he has created for himself. Nvidia's board of directors has launched an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government. Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees. Nvidia stock fell 4.27% on Monday as a dark cloud settled over the company and its once-Teflon CEO's future. Shares were down more than 4% in early trading on Tuesday. Tech investor Dan Niles of Niles Investment Management said this is a "horrible" situation for Huang, someone he has known for 30 years. "[Huang's] got a very deep bench, and a historical example is what happened to Apple after Steve Jobs passed away. … Did it collapse?" Niles said on Sozzi Unleashed. "So Jensen's done a great job of empowering people underneath him. I think one thing that will happen is there will be a successor appointed. The board will force that. And so I think that will occur out of this." "Are the products in the pipeline, much like when Steve Jobs passed away, that will keep the company going for the next couple of years? Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is at the center of a massive scandal that's rocking the AI giant's stock. It's also raising fresh questions about the company's relationship with China — and its stance on selling advanced technology to an economic adversary. Huang admitted in a Nov. 8 memo to employees to an affair following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang (obviously no relation), whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. Nvidia's board has initiated an investigation. Wall Street reaction so far has been negative but not catastrophic, with analysts questioning whether Huang will stay on while acknowledging how central he is to the company and the broader AI revolution. (Here's a suite of reactions.) A key lesson in key-man risk if we've ever seen one. But most critically, the Huang Affair has made it impossible to know where Beijing's alleged intelligence scheme ends and Nvidia's genuine policy aims begin. Everything is now in question. In lobbying for looser export controls with China, was Huang motivated by revenue streams or an illicit romance? Getting entangled in a Chinese spy plot blurs the lines between the company's actual beliefs and what Chinese intelligence officials attempted to accomplish, sowing confusion in markets and the government. "Regardless of the outcome of the investigation, however, we necessarily see Jensen losing some of his power/credibility in advocating for AI and Nvidia with US government representatives," Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson wrote. It's hard to know and implausible to argue the difference between Nvidia's financial interests and China's intelligence scheme. Even if the alleged Chinese spy had zero influence on Huang's decision making and extracted zero intelligence from him and his company, Huang's messiness makes Nvidia appear impaired. But Huang's importance atop the AI mountain makes him a crucial player in the US economy. President Trump and leaders in the tech world have come to his defense. The logic behind it is that Huang is so pivotal to American AI competitiveness that not even his irresponsible actions outweigh his worth and standing as a tech leader. But Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a note on Monday that the investigation will boost major scrutiny of Nvidia and tip the thorny China chip export issue further toward bipartisanship. "On the heels of last week's Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China," he said. (Bloomberg) -- Nvidia Corp.'s (NVDA) general counsel intervened in a US government probe of suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, questioning whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining an executive from the Singapore-based firm who's now at the heart of a scandal threatening Jensen Huang. Nvidia Scandal Creates Risk for AI Industry, Not Just CEO Georgia State Race Reversed After Votes Surface on Memory Card Alice Huang, Suspected China Spy, Spent Years in Nvidia's Orbit Several Senate Republicans Call for Delaying Leadership Election CoreWeave Asks Texas Governor-Elect for Data Center Cooperation In late summer 2025, Nvidia's Tim Teter called Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees US chip export curbs, to ask about the Megaspeed investigation, according to people familiar with the matter. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Specifically, Teter wanted to know whether Kessler's Bureau of Industry and Security was involved in the Singapore government's recent detention of Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, according to the people. Singapore police had brought Alice in for questioning and restricted her from leaving the country. BIS was not involved in that action, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity owing to the sensitivity of the matter. Jensen on Sunday admitted to having an affair with Alice after previously lying about the nature of their relationship, which is now the subject of an investigation by Nvidia's board. An Nvidia spokesperson said that Teter was unaware of the affair at the time he called Kessler about Alice's detention in Singapore. It's unclear whether Teter made any specific requests of Kessler related to his agency's investigation into Megaspeed, which was separate from Singapore's. But in the weeks that followed, BIS staff were muzzled in their ability to look into the company, including a mandate that they route all requests of Nvidia through Kessler or seek his approval for outreach — a highly unusual step that remains unique to the chipmaker, the people said. They were also told not to mention Megaspeed or Speedmatrix, the company's Malaysian subsidiary, in external communications. Teter, meanwhile, reached out directly to the agency's staff, including requesting a meeting with one of them, according to some of the people. That BIS employee declined the meeting, and Teter responded that he didn't understand why his request was spurned, since Kessler had granted him permission to communicate with BIS employees. It's unclear exactly what Teter wanted to discuss with these individuals. The employees forwarded the email to Kessler, who told them hours later to continue handling the case by the book, to which the employees responded: "10-4. Thank you." Kessler didn't otherwise weigh in on how the employees should proceed with the case, according to one of the people. The New York Times reported earlier on Teter's outreach to BIS employees and their exchange with Kessler. "BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book," a spokesperson for the agency said. "BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high." In late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working on the case with BIS — standard practice for any BIS investigation that turns into a criminal probe — requested that BIS pause its efforts, the people said. BIS has not made any progress since then, despite the agency having enough evidence to move forward. It's an extraordinary episode that raises questions about Nvidia's ability to influence US investigations into breaches of China chip curbs, as well as what exactly Teter sought to do with any additional information about Alice's detention in Singapore. An Nvidia spokesperson, asked about the company's intervention in BIS's Megaspeed probe, said that Nvidia consults with government officials "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups." "We work to resolve any allegations of 'diversion' promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide," the spokesperson said. "Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding US policy and hurt American economic and national security." Despite that stance, in the months after Teter's initial call with Kessler, Nvidia gave BIS an incomplete account of its business with Megaspeed. After several visits to Megaspeed's data centers — 12 facilities owned by eight companies across three countries in Southeast Asia — Nvidia had sent inventory checks to the agency and declared to Bloomberg News in mid-November 2025 that everything was where it should be. The company also said at the time that it had asked the US government whether it needed to cut off business with Megaspeed, and was told no. But Nvidia's tabulations, as relayed to the US government, undercounted the number of chips it had sold to Megaspeed via hardware partners by 50,000 units, according to trade records analyzed by Bloomberg. That's worth billions of dollars. After being pressed about the gap, Nvidia told Bloomberg in December 2025 that it had checked additional Megaspeed warehouses that contained the missing hardware, while declining to state exactly how many chips it found in those facilities or provide any further details. Nvidia also declined to comment on significant additional discrepancies in Megaspeed's data center footprint, including that two of the eight data center operators Nvidia told officials in Washington it had visited said they did not, in fact, have Megaspeed's hardware — and that Megaspeed boasts something of a Chinese corporate twin. It's unclear whether Nvidia has communicated with BIS or DOJ on these topics. Since then, the largest of Megaspeed's data center landlords dropped Megaspeed as a tenant. Nvidia, for its part, has consistently declined to comment on whether it has completed any additional visits to that site or any of Megaspeed's other facilities, despite pledging to do so nearly a year ago. BIS, meanwhile, has declined to impose restrictions on Nvidia's ability to do business with the firm despite calls for such a step from senior levels of the Trump administration. Megaspeed has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations, and said that its outreach to the US government about the probe has gone unanswered. The company added that Singapore's investigation "into activities related to alleged chip diversion concluded earlier this year with no adverse action against Megaspeed." Bloomberg has been unable to reach Alice Huang despite repeated attempts over the past year. Megaspeed was not speaking on her behalf. Around three months ago, Nvidia's Teter had a call with someone else on Trump's team — an official at the White House. He told this official, according to a person familiar with the call, that Alice is not as important in Megaspeed as she makes herself out to be, a likely reference to her statement on LinkedIn that she is the company's CEO even though she doesn't hold and has never held that role on paper. Still, because of the bad publicity surrounding Alice, Teter continued, Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed. That bad publicity began in October 2025, when The New York Times first reported that the US government was looking into the company. In November 2025, Malaysian trade records show, Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia's GB300s processors, at the time the most advanced and sought after AI chips on the market, worth some $787 million. Today, Megaspeed remains an official Nvidia Cloud Partner — a coveted designation in the data center world that Nvidia generally takes away from companies when they no longer do business with those firms. title: Nvidia sells off for second day in fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged spy - CNBC
content:
Nvidia shares sank 5.47% on Tuesday as investors continued to weigh the potential fallout from CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The embattled chip giant briefly dipped below $4 trillion in market cap during afternoon trading, but bounced back to close above that level. Nvidia last cleared the $4 trillion benchmark on July 9, 2025. Shares closed more than 4% lower on Monday, the day after Huang told staff in an email that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and had “fallen short” of his responsibilities as CEO. He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that U.S. officials had concluded she was “a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing” and “possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China.” U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating. “I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.” Adding to the tech giant’s woes was a class-action shareholder lawsuit filed against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California. The Rosen Law Firm’s suit alleges the defendants made false or misleading statements about his affair with Huang and Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, thereby presenting a material risk to the company’s reputation and business prospects. “Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the Board investigation is completed,” said Dan Ives, senior and managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, in a Tuesday note. “We would expect a Board investigation that could take 4 weeks to 6 weeks and will create a clear overhand on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.” Amid Nvidia’s turmoil, some of its chip rivals are seeing a boost. Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom built on a strong start to the week, with AMD gaining 1.3% and Broadcom adding nearly 4%. AMD gained 13% on Monday, while Broadcom added just over 10%. — CNBC’s Dan Mangan and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. title: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls - TradingView
content: China’s top AI startup Moonshot AI accessed Nvidia's most advanced servers this summer, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing documents filed with Beijing regulators – a development that could intensify scrutiny of the chipmaker as it reels from fallout over its CEO’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The firm behind the Kimi K3 AI technology signed a contract in August to rent 32 Super Micro Computer (SMCI) servers equipped with Nvidia’s B300 GPUs, the most powerful AI accelerators on the market, according to the report. The online filings valued the servers at 432 million yuan ($64.8 million) and said they were located in China, indicating a possible breach of U.S. rules that forbid sales to the country without an explicit license. Moonshot disputed the documents' accuracy. After Bloomberg contacted the company for comment, the documents no longer referenced Moonshot. The report comes close to the heels of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair with a person U.S. authorities suspect to be a Chinese spy. The admission has created a financial shock, with analysts panicking that Huang, a key force behind the AI boom, might lose his CEO title. On Monday, a law firm filed a class action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang for misleading investors, and Delaware senator Chris Coons called for a congressional investigation on national security grounds. NVDA shares were up 2% in the overnight session after a sharp slide on Monday, while Intel (INTC) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) were down 0.8% and 0.4%, respectively. Nvidia management is expected to face a barrage of questions about the controversy at its earnings report on Nov. 17. Deepwater Asset Management’s managing partner Gene Munster said China’s alleged targeting of Nvidia's CEO is a greater risk than meets the eye. “The fact that China targeted Jensen underscores the geopolitical significance of AI leadership. That means both Democrats and Republicans will need to build lots of data centers,” Munster said in an X post. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA inched up multiple points in the ‘extremely bullish’ zone amid ‘extremely high’ message volume. “$NVDA just some noise. Cheap stock,” a trader posted. At least 57% of the traders who voted in an ongoing Stocktwits poll said they are buying the dip in NVDA after the company announced the investigation into Huang’s affair. Fifteen percent said they were trimming their position, while an equal share said they were waiting for the investigation results before deciding what they thought of the stock. After Monday’s drop, Nvidia shares slid into the red for 2026 and are down 4%. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. title: Trump says Jensen Huang told him Monday he didn't know paramour 'was a spy' - CNBC
content:
President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, and that Huang denied knowing that the woman he admitted having an extramarital affair with “was a spy” for China. Trump told reporters at the White House that he was “amazed” by the allegations against Huang, which led Nvidia’s board to initiate an independent investigation. Trump suggested he had only recently learned of allegations that Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said. “I asked him today because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right. ‘How you doing?’” Trump said. “And I asked him about that, and he ...  said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’ ” The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that Alice Huang had been eyed by U.S. spy agencies “for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to  China,” and that “American officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.” The Times reported that about a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings “and chose not to do anything with the information.” The newspaper noted that Trump has been reluctant to disrupt chip sales by Nvidia, which are boosting the U.S. stock market. On Friday, The Times reported that a memo that circulated last spring among top Trump administration policymakers “cited intelligence that a Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.” The Times said the memo reported that Alice Huang was recruited to collect intelligence on the Nvidia CEO “as part of a drive by Beijing’s top spy agency to learn more about American A.I. chips and potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” “I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago,” Trump said Monday. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.” Trump on Monday said of Jensen Huang, “He’s suffering greatly.” “I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement, and I believe he’s suffering greatly, more so because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family. But he is definitely suffering.” Asked if he would bring up the issue involving Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet next week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen,  China, Trump said, “I don’t think so.” “I mean, maybe I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it,” Trump said. “I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable, honorable man. I mean ... he built a great company,  American company, and I think he’s a very honorable guy, and I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.” Trump’s comments came as a Los Angeles law firm filed a class-action shareholder lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California. The Rosen Law Firm’s suit alleges the defendants made false or misleading statements about his affair with Huang and Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, which presented a material risk to the company’s reputation and business prospects. It has never priced one at a company worth more than $4 trillion that makes up nearly 7% of the S&P 500 (^GSPC). Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang admitted in a Nov. 8 memo to employees to an affair following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. The board has opened an independent investigation. Nvidia stock fell about 4% Monday to its lowest close since April, even as the PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) jumped nearly 7%. That's its worst showing against the chip index since January 2019, by Yahoo Finance calculations. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. The scale is hard to overstate. At Friday's close, Nvidia was worth about four times the nine biggest companies ever hit by CEO personal-conduct scandals combined, by Yahoo Finance calculations. The largest, Intel (INTC), was worth $249 billion when Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a past consensual relationship with an employee. Nvidia was about 18 times that. This is key-person risk — the danger that a company's value rests on one person — at its most extreme. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has run it ever since, with no named successor. Adjust for a bigger stock market, and the gap narrows but doesn't close. No earlier scandal-hit company made up more than about 1% of the S&P 500, a mark only Intel in 2018 and HP (HPQ) in 2010 reached. Nvidia is about seven times that. History puts a price on it. A 2018 study in the Journal of Financial Economics found stocks fell about 4% on average when the CEO was the one caught. At Nvidia's size, that's roughly $185 billion, more than McDonald's (MCD) was worth when it fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Nvidia lost about $190 billion in market value Monday. Until Monday, Wall Street had treated Nvidia like the safe chip stock. Through Friday's close, Nvidia had fallen about 13% since Oct. 28, the last close before The New York Times' first spy report. The chip index dropped about 20% over that stretch, which included a post-midterm rout. Spy stories can hit hard. Super Micro Computer (SMCI) lost 41% in a day in 2018 on a report of Chinese spy chips in its servers, a report that was never confirmed. The closer precedent may be Intel's Lip-Bu Tan. In August 2025, President Trump said Tan should resign over Tan's China ties. Within a month, Washington had taken a stake in Intel, and the stock was up about 20%. This time, Trump is in the CEO's corner. "I think he's an honorable guy," he told reporters Sunday. That could become its own problem. The bigger questions in Congress "are going to be about Nvidia's relationship with Trump and Trump's relationship with Nvidia," Chris Miller, a professor at Tufts University's Fletcher School and author of "Chip War," told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "If it's true that the president had this intelligence for some time, but declined to act on it, that will be a focus of investigation," he said. Options traders are bracing for more. Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, and the next day the Republican chairs of three House committees want Huang at a closed-door briefing. Friday's prices for options expiring Nov. 18 implied a swing of about 11% either way by then. Over a similar stretch around its last eight earnings reports, Nvidia moved about 4% on average, by Yahoo Finance calculations. "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA," spokesperson John Rizzo said. We are also looking at Neoclouds expanding to serve enterprises and sovereign customers. Management expects those buyers to drive sequential growth, with hyperscaler growth reaccelerating afterward as Rubin supply improves. I'll be watching shipment conversion closely because customers can't generate revenue until Nvidia delivers the equipment. Gross margins need attention too. Management expects 74% in Q3, down from 75%, as memory costs surge. Q4 could fall to 71%–72%. Those remain exceptional margins, and higher volumes can support earnings despite the pressure. Guidance also assumes no China Data Center compute revenue. Any permitted sales could help, although I wouldn't rely on them. Now, I believe Nvidia's growth will extend beyond this upcoming quarter. Several recent announcements point in that direction. Oracle's (ORCL) October 27 expansion targets multi-gigawatt Vera Rubin infrastructure. Google's (GOOGL) A5X infrastructure is designed to scale to 960,000 Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) across multiple sites, with general availability planned this month. These are long-term deployment plans. Meanwhile, Meta (META) is expanding Rubin and Vera central processing unit (CPU) deployments around Muse. Those plans support demand beyond training. Running agents and improving models through reinforcement learning require substantial compute. Physical AI also adds robotics workloads. Nvidia also captures spending on networking and CPUs alongside GPUs, while Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) supports customers across hardware generations. The physical rollout should improve too. DSX POD modular factories can be installed in as little as 14 days, with deliveries planned for early 2027. That applies to prepared sites with supporting infrastructure. Of course, it doesn't eliminate permitting or power requirements. Still, faster installation helps turn spending into usable capacity. Management expects roughly 70% Fiscal 2028 revenue growth, with supply constrained through that year. It's also worth mentioning that October's capacity agreements target a 2.5x substrate expansion over three years. Manufacturing partners are making long-term commitments to meet Nvidia's requirements. Expansion is increasingly global. Google is adding European availability, while Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN plans further Blackwell and Rubin deployments. I believe this gives Nvidia customers outside the U.S. a construction cycle. Now, to be fair, the Democratic congressional sweep has intensified regulatory fears. This is especially true around electricity costs and development restrictions. However, Congress generally doesn't approve individual data centers. Zoning decisions usually sit locally, while environmental permitting and grid connections involve separate authorities. State leadership therefore matters. So, sure, Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants development paused pending protections, and local ballot measures favored restrictions. Delays could hurt deliveries, including contracted projects. However, I think markets are assuming too much demand disappears. Developers can relocate projects, although that takes time. Meta's Prometheus first phase is already complete. Existing infrastructure and international projects leave considerable demand moving forward. Nvidia's valuation looks increasingly attractive after the recent sell-off. At today's price, Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $9.31 implies 20.04x earnings. Fiscal 2028's $15.91 estimate brings that to roughly 12x. Forecasts of $21.34 for Fiscal 2029 and $25.98 for Fiscal 2030 imply 8.74x and 7.19x. Expected EPS growth slows from roughly 95% this year to 71%, then 34% and 22%. Those are demanding forecasts, especially further out. Nevertheless, even, say, a 30% shortfall against Fiscal 2028 consensus leaves $11.14 EPS and a 17.1x multiple. Of course, such a misstep is highly unlikely. Regardless, I find even that multiple reasonable for Nvidia's competitive position. Its net-cash balance sheet supports continued investment. CUDA and its networking platform help customers deploy whole systems efficiently. Earnings growth can support returns without a higher multiple. Better shipment execution could also raise estimates. In any case, there are a number of risks to keep in mind. Hyperscalers could moderate capex if AI returns disappoint. Google and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators threaten some workloads, while AMD (AMD) competes for customers. Memory inflation could exceed current assumptions. Nvidia's enormous expected scale also makes shares sensitive to any disappointment. A strong quarter alone cannot remove those risks. Nvidia stock has a Strong Buy consensus, based on 33 Buy ratings. The average price target of $323.45 implies 73% upside from today's share price. I remain bullish ahead of Q3. Political obstacles can slow construction, but customer deployments suggest the compute shortage persists. Around 12x Fiscal 2028 earnings looks unusually attractive to me. Nvidia can deliver compelling returns through earnings growth, provided customers keep converting their AI ambitions into operating capacity. title: Nvidia vs. Alphabet: The AI Revolution Is Big Enough for Both. Here's the Better Buy. - The Motley Fool
content: Which part of the AI trade is more likely to better serve investors? The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution keeps delivering winning stocks driven by that technology. Since AI encompasses so many niches within tech, it will make numerous investors better off, and the gains will not be limited to just one investment. Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) and Google's parent company, Alphabet (GOOGL -0.27%) (GOOG -0.38%), are two notable winners. The latest iteration of AI is built on Nvidia's hardware, while Alphabet has long innovated in the field, and the success of its most notable businesses relies heavily on AI. Still, between the two tech stocks, I believe Alphabet may have the slightly brighter future. Here's why. Admittedly, it is difficult to go against Nvidia in any AI race. Its AI accelerators power generative AI, and while other competitors have emerged over time, Nvidia's hardware remains dominant. In the first two quarters of fiscal 2027 (ended July 26), that dominance drove a 96% year-over-year increase in revenue for the company. This is not an anomaly, as the growth of Nvidia's AI accelerator business has been unprecedented in recent years. Amid that growth, the stock has gained 1,460% from its October 2022 low. That gave it the world's largest market cap and a surprisingly modest price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23, below the S&P 500 average earnings multiple of 26. Nonetheless, the immediate problem is how the company has driven this growth. Increasingly, Nvidia has loaned money to customers to buy equipment. Should some of them declare bankruptcy, the company could be in for massive write-offs. According to its latest 10-Q filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), 70% of its accounts receivable balance comes from just five customers. Amid that lack of diversification, this is not a concern Nvidia investors should dismiss. In contrast, Alphabet appears poised to benefit from present and future growth, though that comes with some challenges. Since Nvidia's 2022 low, Alphabet stock has risen by a more modest 190%. Moreover, its $160 billion in capital expenditures (capex) may seem concerning. The free cash outflows during the last two quarters and the sudden need to increase borrowing may worry shareholders who bought Alphabet for its financial stability. Alphabet appears to surpass Nvidia in unrealized growth potential. With that, its spending may be paying off, and one way is in the growth of Google Cloud. Alphabet's overall revenue grew 24% in the first nine months of 2026. However, that pales in comparison to Google Cloud's 84% revenue increase for the same period. Additionally, Google Cloud generates 21% of the company's revenue. In contrast, Nvidia's data center segment accounts for more than 92% of its revenue. Although Alphabet also finances some of its customers, these percentages suggest it is less exposed to this risk than Nvidia. Furthermore, Alphabet's next great revenue stream could come from Waymo, its autonomous driving company. CEO Sundar Pichai believes Waymo could "meaningfully contribute" to the company's revenue as soon as 2027. While this will almost certainly take years to materialize, it is likely not figured into Alphabet's stock price, leaving considerable room for growth. Finally, investors can buy this stock right now for just 15 times earnings. That valuation arguably makes it worth buying on this pullback. Nvidia and Alphabet are both doing their part to power the AI revolution, but while nobody should discount Nvidia's successes, Alphabet's stock seems to offer greater future growth potential. This comes down to two factors: data center exposure and Waymo's growth. Although Alphabet could get hit if some of its customers go bankrupt, its exposure is a small fraction of what Nvidia faces. Moreover, the Waymo growth story has not yet really started, suggesting the Google parent could experience a huge revenue surge in the coming years. The PRICE of GOLD rose on Monday amid a weaker US Dollar and falling crude oil prices following last week's 'blue wave' midterms election results, while some AI-related shares recovered from last week's tech sell-off, writes Atsuko Whitehouse at BullionVault. Giant AI chipmaker Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) slid however in US pre-market trading after CEO Jensen Huang was accused of dating a Chinese government spy, while protests against data centres continued in Europe over the weekend. Gold last week gained 3.5%, rebounding from end-October's 13-month low after the US midterm elections resulted in the Democrat Party winning control of both the Senate and the House, but paring gains Friday following stronger-than-expected US jobs data. The Nasdaq Composite ended the week 3.4% lower, its fourth consecutive weekly decline, despite rallying 1.1% on Friday after Thursday's steep tech stock sell-off. The Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterms mean concerns about tighter regulation of AI and data centres "hit a market already nervous on AI capex", says Nicky Shiels, head of metals strategy at Swiss gold bullion refining and finance group MKS Pamp. Bloomberg Opinion columnist John Authers points to investor concerns that the US midterm election results could "make it harder to build AI data centers." By the close on 6 November, the Nasdaq Composite was 10.9% below its 6 October all-time closing high. Over the same period, gold fell 2.6% in US Dollar terms, based on the LBMA's London afternoon auction benchmark. Gold also fell in the early stages of the Dot-Com bust in 2000, though by far less than the Nasdaq Composite. In the 5 weeks after New Year's tech-stock index peaked on 10 March 2000, the Nasdaq fell 34.2%, while gold slipped 2.8%. By the time the Nasdaq Composite reached its Tech Crash closing low on 9 October 2002, the index was down 77.9% from its peak, while gold traded 10.0% above its level on 10 March 2000. Spot gold prices for London settlement today rose as much as 2.1% to $4134 per troy ounce in early Asian trading, peaking below Friday's near-3-week high before easing to $4085 and then rising again to $4115 by lunchtime in the UK, some 1.6% above Friday's afternoon auction price. The Dollar Index – a measure of the US currency's value versus its major rich-world peers – slipped 0.4%, curbing the gains in gold for UK and Euro investors. Brent crude oil meanwhile fell 2.0% to $96.29 a barrel as traders weighed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, extending last week's 16% drop, its steepest since the Covid Crash of April 2020. Most Asian stock markets rose on Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining 2.3% for its first rise in six sessions. But South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi fell 0.8% to its lowest close since 2 February, leaving it 44.9% below its June record high, even as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix edged higher. Nvidia shares fell 4.5% in premarket trading after the company responded to media reports of an extra-marital affair by opening an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence 'honey trap' operation. Finding increasing demand from the electrical and electronics industries, silver today rose as much as 2.8% to $53.46 per troy ounce before easing to $52.64, still 1.2% above Friday's London auction price. Silver prices gained 3.8% last week, recovering from a nearly 13-month low in US Dollar terms, but fellow electrical-and-electronics metal copper fell 2.7% on the London Metal Exchange, rallying on Monday as investors weigh the risk of a slowdown in US or European data centre construction. LME three-month copper has now lost over 7.0% since hitting a record $14,875 per tonne on 10 September.
